impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache with humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent scope, particularly for genus claims in the biologics space where specifications disclose one embodiment but claim a broader class.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to enforce genus claims in the biologics and pharmaceutical space, even when the specification discloses only a single species, so long as the prior art and specification together support the breadth of the claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Increases litigation risk for generic and biosimilar drug manufacturers who may face broader patent infringement claims based on genus-level patent claims covering classes of biologics.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on customers' exclusive purchase of the patent holder's unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, even when the tied products may have non-infringing uses.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding Ingevity liable for unlawful tying under the Sherman Act for conditioning licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court held that whether the honeycomb products had substantial non-infringing uses was properly a jury question, and the jury's finding of antitrust liability was supported by sufficient evidence.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides competitors with a strong precedent to challenge patent holders who leverage patent rights to force exclusive purchasing arrangements for unpatented products in adjacent markets.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face significant antitrust liability risk if they condition patent licenses on exclusive purchase of unpatented products, particularly where those products have substantial uses outside the patent's scope.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions via emulating program behavior and comparing function calls to a model are abstract under step one of the Alice framework, and whether damages for patent infringement may include sales to customers outside the United States.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million patent infringement judgment against Gen Digital (Norton), holding that the asserted claims of Columbia's cybersecurity patents are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, reinforcing the presumption against extraterritorial application of U.S. patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies with stronger defenses against broadly-claimed software patents, particularly in cybersecurity, and limits patent damages exposure from foreign sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: University and research institution patent holders may find it harder to enforce software-related patents and recover damages on global product sales.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content presentation specifications to a wireless device's capabilities are ineligible for patenting under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's streaming media patents, which claim methods of tailoring content delivery to a device's screen size and capabilities, are ineligible under § 101 as directed to abstract ideas. The ruling reversed a jury verdict of infringement and a $2.5 million damages award against Netflix, entering judgment for Netflix on all claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies operating streaming and content delivery services benefit from the narrowing of patent eligibility for claims covering conventional content adaptation techniques.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with software-related patents claiming adaptive content delivery face heightened invalidity risk under § 101, potentially devaluing existing patent portfolios in the streaming technology space.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to selecting a processor core based on measured processing speed parameters are limited in scope by extraterritoriality principles when the accused products are designed domestically but manufactured and sold abroad, and whether the district court properly struck damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed-in-part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel, finding that the extraterritoriality analysis was improperly applied. The court also reversed the striking of VLSI's damages expert theories. The case was remanded for further proceedings, keeping alive a potentially significant damages claim against Intel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a broader interpretation of domestic infringement theories when accused products are designed in the U.S. but manufactured abroad, and from greater latitude in presenting damages evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor and technology companies with global manufacturing operations face increased exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims even when production occurs overseas.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact preclude summary judgment on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim alleging attempted monopolization through a fraudulently obtained patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims in a dispute over coiled tubing patents, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case was remanded for trial, keeping alive both the patent unenforceability defense and the antitrust counterclaim alleging that Tenaris attempted to monopolize the coiled tubing market through patents obtained by fraud.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors gain a stronger path to pursue Walker Process antitrust claims when there is evidence that a patent holder concealed material prior art during prosecution.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face dual exposure to both patent unenforceability and antitrust liability when prior art concealment during prosecution is plausibly alleged.

impacts.caseName: Apple Inc. v. International Trade Commission
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated § 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated § 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygenation measurement devices. The court upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models, affirming the ITC's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the medical device and wearable technology space are affirmed in their ability to use ITC proceedings to obtain import exclusion orders against major technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant commercial disruption from ITC exclusion orders when incorporating patented health-monitoring technologies into products, potentially requiring product redesign or licensing.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations used in digital communication systems are eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated-in-part the district court's summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of Constellation Designs' patents relating to non-uniform constellations in communication systems, finding that the eligibility analysis was inadequate for some claims. The court affirmed eligibility for other claims, affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, and remanded for further proceedings on the vacated claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the communications standards space retain viable infringement claims where claims are tied to specific technical implementations rather than abstract mathematical concepts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, with mixed eligibility rulings creating uncertainty about the scope of enforceable claims in standards-essential patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge for purposes of establishing the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony from a corporate representative is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and that computer source code commands are not hearsay statements. These evidentiary rulings facilitated the invalidation of patents covering engine controller reprogramming technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from expanded evidentiary tools, including broad admissibility of 30(b)(6) testimony and source code evidence to prove prior art sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges when prior art products were sold by third parties whose current representatives lack firsthand knowledge of the sales.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court abused its discretion by excluding a patent holder's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy without permitting supplemental expert discovery.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft on the ground that Exafer lacked a remedy. The court found that the district court improperly excluded the expert's reasonable royalty analysis and should have permitted Exafer to supplement its damages case through reopened discovery rather than eliminating its claim entirely.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from greater protection against having damages claims dismissed due to technical deficiencies in expert reports, with courts encouraged to allow supplementation rather than exclusion.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent cases may face prolonged litigation as courts are now less likely to grant dispositive motions based on exclusion of damages evidence.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it missed the statutory deadline for seeking a stay of the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that BioMarin could not circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay under § 1659(a) by voluntarily dismissing its original declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one after the stay deadline had passed. This prevents gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court proceedings involving pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent challengers benefit from certainty that parallel district court litigation cannot be stayed through procedural maneuvering by ITC respondents who missed statutory deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents lose a potential litigation strategy of refiling district court actions to obtain mandatory stays they failed to timely request in the original proceeding.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the PTAB governing discretionary denial of inter partes review institution are 'general statements of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions governing PTAB discretionary denial of IPR institution are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking. The court emphasized that Congress provided no legal right to IPR institution and that the Director retains ultimate authority over institution decisions, making the challenged instructions non-binding policy guidance.
impacts.positiveImplications: The PTO retains broad flexibility to issue and revise IPR institution guidance without formal rulemaking, providing administrative efficiency in managing patent review proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies seeking to challenge patents through IPR face continued uncertainty from discretionary denials governed by policy guidance that cannot be challenged through APA rulemaking requirements.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to district court patent litigation may file IPR petitions challenging the same patents on the statutory deadline applicable to the actual litigant, and whether the Board properly determined obviousness of claims requiring reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding errors in the Board's analysis of claims requiring reporting shipment sensor information after a time delay. The court also addressed concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed on behalf of actual litigants to circumvent the one-year filing bar.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from scrutiny of potential proxy IPR petitions filed by non-parties to circumvent statutory filing deadlines, and from more rigorous Board analysis of obviousness challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third parties to file IPR petitions face increased risk that such petitions may be challenged as improper attempts to circumvent the statutory time bar.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff met its burden to establish that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation, holding that the plaintiff failed to show its asserted trade secrets regarding cosmetic penile implant design were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship finding on the same basis, while affirming liability for counterfeiting related to unauthorized trademark use.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending against trade secret claims benefit from a rigorous standard requiring plaintiffs to demonstrate that asserted secrets are not generally known in the relevant industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs face heightened burden to prove their information is truly secret and not merely a compilation of generally known techniques.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC's practice of automatically designating all questionnaire responses in antidumping and countervailing duty investigations as confidential is consistent with the governing statute, and whether 19 U.S.C. § 1516a abrogates the common law right of public access to judicial records.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the ITC's blanket practice of automatically designating all questionnaire responses as confidential in trade investigations is incompatible with the statute, and that 19 U.S.C. § 1516a does not abrogate the common law right of public access to court records. The decision requires the ITC to make individualized confidentiality determinations rather than applying automatic designations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies and trade associations gain greater transparency into trade remedy proceedings, with potential access to previously confidential questionnaire data that could inform business decisions and competitive intelligence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies responding to ITC questionnaires in antidumping and countervailing duty investigations face increased risk that their commercially sensitive business information may become publicly accessible.
